title: Thieves Snatch $4.6M Diamond Necklace From Viennese Museum
description:
News
                The two thieves paid entry before stealing the 673- white diamond necklace that once belonged to Queen Nazl
body:
News
                The two thieves paid entry before stealing the 673- white diamond necklace that once belonged to Queen Nazli of Egypt.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            An exhibition view of GLANZSTÜCKE: Van Cleef & Arpels High Jewelry × Masterpieces from the MAK Collection (2026) shows the necklace that was stolen from the museum. (© Van Cleef & Arpels; courtesy Museum of Applied Arts, Vienna)
    
        
            Two visitors smashed a display case and made off with a platinum and diamond necklace at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna yesterday afternoon, August 27. Per the Viennese daily newspaper Der Standard, the Van Cleef & Arpels necklace was last appraised at $4.6 million by Sotheby's. It was displayed as part of Glanzstücke, an ongoing exhibition featuring over 500 works gathered from the museum's design collection and the French luxury jewelry house. The 200-karat, 673-white diamond necklace was designed in 1939 for Egyptian Queen Nazli on the occasion of her daughter Princess Fawzia's marriage to Iranian Prince Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became Iran's last shah.A press statement from the museum confirmed the theft, but officials declined to comment further due to the ongoing investigation. Austrian media outlets reported that the two men paid for their ticketed entry into the museum before approaching the display case containing the necklace, a set of earrings, and a double-clip brooch from the same collection, along with two decorative wares.

title: Demolition of Georgian Architectural Landmark Sparks Outcry
description:
News
                Civilians, architects, and members of the preservationist community are advocating to save the complex know
body:
News
                Civilians, architects, and members of the preservationist community are advocating to save the complex known locally as the Rike Tubes in the capital city Tbilisi.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Rike Park Music Theatre and Exhibition Hall in Tbilisi, Georgia (Courtesy Levan Davlianidze via Wikimedia Commons, CC-BY-4.0)
    
        
            Demolitions are underway on the Rike Park Music Theatre and Exhibition Hall in Tbilisi, Georgia, prompting outcry from local community members and the architects who designed the two-structure complex. Set against the historic 19th-century buildings that define the capital city's dominant style, the landmark is known as the “Rike Tubes” for its futuristic appearance, a reminder of the country’s modernist push from the 2000s to the early 2010s.The Tbilisi City Hall’s Architectural Service issued the demolition permit in June to the owner, Rike Dom, with the dismantling process commencing last month and due to wrap up by December. In interviews with Reuters and local outlets, many expressed concerns with the decision, describing the tourist hotspot as a defining feature of the capital city skyline.Italian architects Massimiliano and Doriana Fuksas, of Fuksas Studio, were asked to design the complex for musical performance and contemporary art exhibitions in 2010, under then-Prime Minister Nika Gilauri and United National Movement (UNM) President Mikheil Saakashvili (who has been in prison for nearly five years for abuse of power charges). Construction began on the glass-and-steel tubes in 2011. When the conservative Georgian Dream party came into power in 2012, officials froze construction, leaving the project unfinished.

title: The Belgian Exhibition That Strives to "Decenter" the West
description:
Art Review
                With two contradictory briefs — to both decenter Europe and show Bruges’s centrality in international
body:
Art Review
                With two contradictory briefs — to both decenter Europe and show Bruges’s centrality in international networks — an exhibition on the Belgian city is already off to a bumpy start.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Installation view of Jan van Eyck, "Portret van Margareta van Eyck" (1439) in Bigger Picture: Connected worlds of Bruges 900-1550 at BRUSK (© Jan Darthet; all images courtesy BRUSK)
    
        
            BRUGES, Belgium — With its cobblestone streets, glossy green canals, and stepped gable townhouses, Bruges has the self-contained and unchanging quality of a scene in a snow globe. Bigger Picture: Connected worlds of Bruges 900-1550 seeks to bust this myth, demonstrating the extent of the city’s historical connection with the rest of the world. The inaugural exhibition of BRUSK — “BRU” for Bruges and “SK” for schone kunsten (“fine art”) — a large new gallery attached to the Groeningemuseum, the show is guest curated by Peter Frankopan, an Oxford medievalist and author of a popular history of the Silk Road. In addition to demonstrating Bruges’s global connections, the exhibition also invokes the notion of decentering the “West” from its self-appointed position as the hub of civilization, via a video presentation, starring Frankopan, that plays at its entry. With these two somewhat contradictory briefs — to both decenter Europe and show Bruges’s centrality in international networks — the exhibition is off to a bumpy start. A further complication is the vast number and type of objects on display: There are over 250 items, ranging from a surprisingly covetable chain mail jacket and underwhelming shreds of ancient silk to significant paintings by Titian, Jan van Eyck, and Hans Memling, as well as religious relics, manuscripts of North African and European origin, Turkish carpets, Viking artifacts, coins, religious garb, and more.Installation view of Bigger Picture: Connected worlds of Bruges 900-1550(© Stad Brugge)To manage this vast range of materials, the exhibition is divided into four “worlds,” each defined by its own intricately designed enclosure delimited by hanging cloth. The “North Sea World,” for instance, is made up of triangular panels that recall sails, while the “Mediterranean World” is under a pavilion-style tent. Each world also has a distinct soundscape — the Mediterranean is evoked by a twitter of birds and the sound of creaking wagon wheels. “The World of Christianity” has bells and more birds. The “World of the Court” is accompanied, like a medieval feast, by gentle plucking on string instruments. In the darkened gallery, the worlds form dramatically lit islands, linked by white lines painted on the floor. Aided by the inventive but not illuminating animations playing in each world, the whole installation is reminiscent of the opening credits for Game of Thrones.
                  
                      
                        Art Review
                      
                      
                        Belgium

title: Maybe This Fall Will Be Kind
description:
Weekly Newsletter
                Yayoi Kusama, Sliman Mansour, and Dolly Parton pass away, and a major Pompeii show comes to th
body:
Weekly Newsletter
                Yayoi Kusama, Sliman Mansour, and Dolly Parton pass away, and a major Pompeii show comes to the US.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            From a high platform in the Broadway Junction station, I see a forlorn cloud hovering over the rooftops of East Brooklyn. The sky around it is perfectly clear. The next morning, I find it still standing in the same spot, but it’s faded, famished. That’s how bad things have gotten: The loneliness epidemic has now reached the clouds. Espresso in Williamsburg, watermelon juice in Ditmas Park, writing session in Ridgewood, soccer camp in Bed-Stuy. At a street corner, a mural by @blkopslife shows a hand holding a famous 1964 photo of Malcom X leaning on the shoulder of his tuxedoed friend, Muhammad Ali. It’s in a Black neighborhood that’s been almost completely gentrified.Dolly Parton suddenly dies at 80. She touched the hearts of millions working nine to five. Sliman Mansour dies at 79. He carried the weight of Palestinian pain on his back. I hope he catches a break in the afterlife. And then Yayoi Kusama follows, passing at 97. She’ll live on for eternity thanks to her Infinity Mirrored Rooms. At lunch, the guy from the falafel place tells me that all humans were created from a single soul. I say that sounds good, but no lettuce for me, please. I fear it more than death these days.    I watch clips of China’s humanoid robot olympics and don’t know whether to be amused or frightened. One robot boxer keeps jumping and kicking long after its head is ripped off. At a cafe, I overhear a businessman on a Zoom call announcing, “We’re going to make a big AI push towards the end of the year.” On the other end of the call I see the workers who will probably be replaced by that AI.I laugh at first when I hear that Vancouver police raided an art gallery because someone mistook a sculpture for a man in need of medical assistance. But then it turns out that passed out men are a common sight in the streets of the opioid crisis-stricken city.  The moon is about to turn full, and a lot of aggression starts to make sense. A place called Insomnia Cookies is ironically most empty at night. Summer is on its hind legs, still acting out. Thousands flee for their lives from a huge wave in Nepal. But fall is pushing in, and I do believe it will be kind. —Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

	
		
			Yayoi Kusama, Artist of Infinities, Dies at 97
		
	
	
		Artist Yayoi Kusama, who channeled psychological phenomena into impossibly kaleidoscopic artworks that enamored millions around the world, died in a hospital in Tokyo on August 14 at the age of 97. The news of her death was announced by her studio and David Zwirner Gallery today, August 26.
      
The labor-intensive quality of her works, combined with a Borgesian fascination with mirrors and the infinite, an openness about mental health struggles, and her ever-present red bob, rendered her an icon closer to a rock star or a spiritual leader than a contemporary artist. | Valentina Di Liscia
	
	
		Read More
	

NewsAn exhibition of artifacts from Pompeii will make its United States debut at the Dallas Museum of Art this December.The Department of State removes Kehinde Wiley’s 2015 commissioned painting from the United States embassy in the Dominican Republic, claiming that the artist’s “violent and racist words and depictions” have no place in the foreign relations agency.Sliman Mansour, a renowned Palestinian painter who chronicled over six decades of his country’s fight for liberation, dies at age 79.Welsh music photographer Justin Thomas is accusing painter Elizabeth Peyton of copyright infringement on his photograph of Liam and Noel Gallagher of the British rock band Oasis.Ex-Pussy Riot Member Margarita Konovalova, who went by the alias Rita Flores, claims she was coerced by Russia to spy on other dissident artists.Mayor Zohran Mamdani announces more than $8.4 million in grants toward nonprofit and small business initiatives, including public art commissions and arts programming.The 70-year-old Chinese dissident artist Gao Zhen gets a three-year prison sentence for his sculptures of communist revolutionary and leader Mao Zedong.Sir Joshua Reynolds’s celebrated “Portrait of Mai (Omai)” will be displayed at the Getty Museum in Los Angeles beginning on September 14.As part of the School of Sexuality Project’s 2026 “Vulva Gala,” artists dressed in handmade vulva costumes paraded down the aisle of a church in Long Beach as part of a community-centered celebration centering on approachable, destigmatized learning.Maya Lin, the architect and artist behind the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, DC, and the Civil Rights Memorial in Alabama, will debut her next public art commission in April 2027 at the University of Texas at Austin.Art Movements: Four Native artists are commissioned for the Counterpublic Triennial, the High Line’s fall lineup, new curators at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, a laid-off Artnet News reporter speaks out, and more.From Our Critics

title: China Pulls Artists from Gwangju Biennale as  ‘Taiwan Pavilion’ Moves Forward
description: The Chinese ambassador to South Korea has ordered China’s artists to withdraw from the 16th Gwangju Biennale, which opens September 5, in protest of
body:
The Chinese ambassador to South Korea has ordered China’s artists to withdraw from the 16th Gwangju Biennale, which opens September 5, in protest of the Gwangju Biennial Foundation allowing Taiwanese exhibitors to participate under the name “Taiwan,” South Korean media reported today. 

	In a meeting with Gwangju Mayor Min Hyung-bae at Gwangju City Hall yesterday, Ambassador Dai Bing expressed his “regret and concern” over the decision to restore the name “Taiwan Pavilion” at the request of Taiwan’s Ministry of Culture, the Munhwa Broadcasting Corporation (MBC) reported. 
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Speaking on behalf of the Chinese Embassy, Dai then demanded Chinese curators and  installation staff to halt their preparations and withdraw from the Hajeongung Art Museum in Gwangju, which was set to host their special exhibition.

	MBC reports that Min told Dai during their meeting that “political considerations should not affect the field of art.”

	The Gwangju Biennale Foundation has been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute with Taiwan for more than year over the renaming of a satellite exhibition from the “Taiwan Pavilion” to the “NTMoFA Pavilion,” referencing its commissioning institution, the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts. The two parties disagreed over the circumstances surrounding the name change, with Taiwan’s Ministry of Culture ultimately accusing the GBF of “political censorship” in an August 15 statement.

	GBF denied allegations that it had acted without Taiwan’s consent in an effort to appease Beijing, which does not recognize the sovereignty of the self-governed island. But the dispute quickly escalated into a reputational crisis for the biennale, with artists from Taiwan and China condemning the name change as a betrayal of its founding ideals. 

	The biennale was established in 1994 to commemorate the 1980 Gwangju Uprising, a deadly chapter in South Korea’s struggle against military rule, during which upwards of 2,300 South Korean civilians were estimated to have been killed.

	On Tuesday, the GBF announced that Taiwan’s exhibition at its September edition can open as the “Taiwan Pavilion,” and be advertised as such in its promotional materials. 
	

	In a statement to the South Korean press, the Gwangju Biennale said, “There is not much time left until the opening on September 5, and we are closely monitoring the situation, hoping the exhibition will proceed smoothly.”

title: Robert Mapplethorpe Foundation Denied Use of Roy Cohn Portrait for New Biography Over Political Concerns
description: The Robert Mapplethorpe Foundation denied the use of a 1981 portrait by the artist of notorious New York lawyer Roy M. Cohn for the cover of a forth
body:
The Robert Mapplethorpe Foundation denied the use of a 1981 portrait by the artist of notorious New York lawyer Roy M. Cohn for the cover of a forthcoming biography, titled American Scoundrel: Roy Cohn‘s Dark Journey from Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump, because of its negative affiliation with the sitting US president, according to the New York Times.

	The portrait in question, simply titled Roy Cohn, captures the lawyer’s striking outward stare and scar-split nose head on, surrounded by a black backdrop, a signature of Mapplethorpe’s images during the final decade of his life.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	At the time it was made, Cohn was the subject of an interview for an issue of Andy Warhol’s Interview magazine. Writer and book editor Steven M.L. Aronson, who authored the piece, convinced Cohn to pose for Mapplethorpe, who was at the peak of his fame at the time. By then, Cohn was a major New York figure who, by day, represented mobsters, moguls, and media barons, including then real estate developer and protégé Donald Trump; by night, he partied at Studio.

	The subject was unusual, yet notable for Mapplethorpe, who during the 1970s turned his lens on New York’s S&M scene, most notably in his “X Portfolio” (1978); in the early ’80s, he was just beginning to start photographing high-profile celebrities, collectors, and artists. Despite being publicly anti-gay, however, Cohn himself was secretly closeted. Before the end of the ’80s, both Cohn and Mapplethorpe died from AIDS-related complications.

	A print of the photograph was acquired by the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and the J. Paul Getty Trust, via a gift from the Mapplethorpe foundation in 2011.

	The Mapplethorpe Foundation, which oversees the artist’s estate and collection, reportedly decided against licensing the image’s use for American Scoundrel, co-authored by Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark, because of President Trump’s negative characterization in the book. As a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit, the foundation is prohibited from engaging in certain political activities and was reportedly concerned that the image’s use on the book cover would be considered a political act. The artist started his eponymous foundation shortly before his death “to protect his work, to advance his creative vision and to promote the causes he cared about,” according to its website.
	

	According to the Times, “the foundation’s board feared that Mr. Trump could retaliate, perhaps by threatening its nonprofit tax status,” if he took offense to his characterization in the book. For his part, Trump has been heavily involved in taking aim at cultural institutions during his second administration, including forcing changes at the Smithsonian Institution and taking control of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

	Bird told the Times he was “thunderstruck” and “outraged” at the foundation’s decision, adding “It’s astonishing that these people are being so cowed, so easily.” The Mapplethorpe declined to comment to the Times about Bird’s comments. (A request for further comment from ARTnews was also not returned.)

	Part of Mapplethorpe’s legacy is a controversy surrounding the censorship of his work. In 1989, months after his death, the now-defunct Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., canceled its presentation of a traveling retrospective because of the inclusion of the “X Portfolio.” The institution had received a grant from the National Endowment for the Arts to realize the exhibition, which conservative politicians took issue with, catapulting Mapplethorpe’s to the center of the era’s culture wars.  

	“The idea that a photograph of a dead mobster lawyer could somehow qualify as political activity, even under the Trump administration, is hard to fathom,” Suzanne Nossel, a former chief executive of the free expression group PEN America, told the Times of the foundation’s decision. “And yet, we’re in an environment where no one feels they can rule anything out.”

title: Robert Indiana’s Maine Home Is for Sale, Despite Late Artist’s Intentions to Make It an Art Space
description: The foundation established by Robert Indiana to preserve his legacy is selling the artist’s longtime home on the Maine island of Vinalhaven, despite
body:
The foundation established by Robert Indiana to preserve his legacy is selling the artist’s longtime home on the Maine island of Vinalhaven, despite instructions in his will that the property be transformed into an art space open to the public.

	The Star of Hope Foundation, as the foundation is called, listed this week Indiana’s former home, a rambling 19th-century Odd Fellows lodge known as the Star of Hope, for $1.4 million, according to the New York Times. A second building Indiana owned, a few doors away, is being offered for $210,000. 
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Indiana, best known for his “LOVE” series, with its iconic tilted O, moved to Vinalhaven in 1978 and spent the next 40 years living in the Star of Hope, a local landmark overlooking the island’s harbor. He died in 2018 at age 89. 

	Indiana had specific plans for the building after his death. His will directed that the Star of Hope be restored “to museum quality” and used as an art environment open to the public for visits, classes and lectures and for the preservation and exhibition of his collection, according to the Times. The artist had established the Star of Hope Foundation to preserve his legacy, and the organization inherited his estate after his death. 

	The foundation initially began working toward that goal, stabilizing and partly renovating the aging building. Now, however, it says its mission would be better served by getting out of the property-management business and putting its resources directly toward artists and arts organizations in Maine.

	“These properties are not our purpose — supporting artists is,” Carole Martin, the foundation’s managing director, told the Times. “Selling these properties allows us to convert those assets into philanthropic capital and put resources directly into Maine’s arts community.”

	The decision has drawn criticism from people who say selling Indiana’s home runs counter to the artist’s wishes. Kevin Lipson, a partner at Venable, the law firm that represented Indiana’s estate in litigation, called the decision “a remarkable repudiation of Robert Indiana’s testamentary intent” in an interview with the Times, adding that Indiana “wanted and expected a museum of some sort on Vinalhaven and that apparently is not in the cards.”
	

	Marjorie Stratton, Vinalhaven’s town manager, who knew Indiana, also questioned the decision. Speaking in a personal capacity, she told the Times that Indiana had discussed using the building for art, education, and research and providing space where young people could work and learn about art.

	“It just makes me sad that this foundation doesn’t seem to be following through with what he told me he wanted that to be,” Stratton said.

	The Star of Hope was in rough shape by the time Indiana died. Its paint was peeling, clapboards were rotting, and a tarp covered a leaking roof, according to the Times. The foundation subsequently addressed some of these concerns, repairing its Mansard roof and restoring its windows and doors. But photographs accompanying the current listing show an interior still in various states of disrepair, including peeling paint, exposed framing and lath. 

	The foundation said the building continues to present structural and regulatory problems and described selling it as a practical way to redirect its resources.

	“We are one of many organizations trying to solve a hard problem — how to bring new life to a building that has sat empty for years,” Martin told the Times, adding that selling the property while investing directly in local artists and organizations was “the most honest path forward.”
	

	Not everyone on Vinalhaven opposes the move. Elaine Crossman, who also knew Indiana and owns a motel and art gallery on the town’s Main Street, told the Times that the renovation appeared to have become an expensive quagmire. She hopes a new owner might return the building to active use, including reopening its first-floor storefronts.

	“I’m optimistic that this is actually a really positive move,” Crossman said. “My hope would be that this is a big step in the right direction for that group to be able to do some positive work in the community.”

schema.headline: Robert Indiana’s Maine Home Is for Sale, Despite Late Artist’s Intentions to Make It an Art Space
